goals: Describe transcription and the processing of hnRNA into mRNA
Define intron, exon, cistron, recon, muton, and monocistronic and polycistronic units
State the discovery and features of the genetic code
Explain initiation, elongation and termination of translation

slides.heading: Gene expression
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a gene’s message is copied into RNA, decoded and turned into protein.

visual.alt: Flow from gene to hnRNA to mature mRNA to polypeptide

slides.narration: A gene is expressed in two main steps. First its message is copied into RNA, which in eukaryotes must be processed before use. Then the RNA message is decoded on ribosomes to make a chain of amino acids.

slides.heading: The transcription unit
slides.body_md: A **transcription unit** has a **promoter** (where RNA polymerase binds), the **structural gene** and a **terminator**. Only the **template strand** (3′→5′) is copied; RNA is made **5′→3′** and matches the **coding strand**, with **U in place of T**.

slides.narration: Only one strand of the gene is copied. If both were copied, two different RNAs would be made, and they would pair with each other and block translation. The other strand, called the coding strand, has the same sequence as the RNA, except that uracil replaces thymine.

slides.heading: Transcription in prokaryotes and eukaryotes
slides.body_md: Transcription runs in three stages: **initiation, elongation and termination**.

rows: Three: I (rRNAs), II (hnRNA, precursor of mRNA), III (tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNAs)
Sigma factor helps the enzyme bind the promoter
Polymerase with other factors binds the promoter
Cytoplasm; translation can start at once

visual.alt: Table comparing transcription in bacteria and eukaryotes

slides.narration: In bacteria a single RNA polymerase, guided by the sigma factor at initiation and the rho factor at termination, makes every kind of RNA. Eukaryotes use three polymerases, and their RNA is made in the nucleus and processed before it reaches the ribosomes.

slides.heading: Processing of hnRNA
slides.body_md: In eukaryotes the primary transcript, **hnRNA**, contains **exons** (coding) and **introns** (non-coding). **Splicing** removes introns and joins exons; **capping** adds **methyl guanosine triphosphate** at the 5′ end; **tailing** adds **200–300 adenylate residues** at the 3′ end.

slides.narration: Only after splicing, capping and tailing does the mature messenger RNA leave the nucleus. The cap and tail protect the message and help the ribosome find it. Genes made of exons and introns are called split genes.

slides.heading: Terms for parts of a gene
slides.body_md: ISC asks for brief definitions of these terms.

rows: Coding sequence that appears in mature mRNA
Intervening non-coding sequence removed by splicing
Segment of DNA coding for one polypeptide
Smallest unit that can mutate (a single nucleotide)
One structural gene per transcription unit (mostly eukaryotes)
Several structural genes in one unit (mostly bacteria, such as the lac operon)

visual.alt: Table of gene terms with meanings

slides.narration: A cistron is a stretch of DNA coding for one polypeptide. The smallest part that can recombine is the recon, and the smallest part that can mutate is the muton. Eukaryotic units usually carry one gene, while bacterial units often carry several.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from template to protein
slides.body_md: The template strand of a short gene reads 3′–TACAAGCCTACCATT–5′. Write the mRNA and the peptide it codes for.
bullets: Pair each template base with its RNA partner (A with U, T with A, G with C, C with G): mRNA 5′–**AUGUUCGGAUGGUAA**–3′.
Read in triplets from AUG: AUG · UUC · GGA · UGG · UAA.
Peptide: **Met–Phe–Gly–Trp**, then stop at UAA.

visual.alt: Worked table: codons and amino acids Met, Phe, Gly, Trp, stop

slides.narration: Write the partner of each template base, using uracil instead of thymine, and remember the new strand runs five prime to three prime. Then split the message into triplets from the start codon and look up each one until you reach a stop codon.

slides.heading: Cracking the genetic code
slides.body_md: With four bases, a **doublet** code gives only 16 words, too few for 20 amino acids; a **triplet** code gives **64**.

rows: Argued that the code must be a triplet
Chemical synthesis of RNA with defined repeats
Cell-free system for protein synthesis to decode codons
Polynucleotide phosphorylase to make RNA without a template

visual.alt: Table of scientists who cracked the genetic code

slides.narration: Gamow reasoned that a code of single bases or pairs of bases could not name twenty amino acids, so each word must have three letters. Khorana’s synthetic messages, Nirenberg’s cell-free system and Ochoa’s enzyme then let the whole code be worked out.

slides.heading: Features of the genetic code
slides.body_md: Of the 64 codons, **61 code for amino acids** and **3 are stop codons**.

rows: One codon codes for only one amino acid
Some amino acids have more than one codon
Same codons in bacteria and humans, with rare exceptions
AUG codes for methionine and starts; UAA, UAG and UGA stop

visual.alt: Table of the features of the genetic code

slides.narration: Because the code is nearly universal, a human gene placed in a bacterium can still be read correctly. Degeneracy means a change in the third base of a codon often leaves the amino acid unchanged.

slides.heading: Translation on the ribosome
slides.body_md: Each **tRNA** is first **charged** with its amino acid (aminoacylation, using ATP). At **initiation**, the small subunit binds mRNA at **AUG** with the initiator tRNA. In **elongation**, a tRNA whose **anticodon** pairs with the codon enters the **A site**, a **peptide bond** forms, and the ribosome moves on one codon. At a **stop codon** a **release factor** ends the process.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: anticodons and a silent change
slides.body_md: An mRNA contains the codons UUU, UUC and GCA. Write the anticodon (3′→5′) of each matching tRNA and the amino acid it carries. What happens to the protein if UUU mutates to UUC?
bullets: Pair each base: A with U, G with C.
UUU → anticodon 3′–AAA–5′ → **Phe**
UUC → anticodon 3′–AAG–5′ → **Phe**
GCA → anticodon 3′–CGU–5′ → **Ala**
UUU and UUC both code for **Phe**, so the protein is unchanged: the code is **degenerate**.

visual.alt: Worked table: anticodons AAA, AAG, CGU

slides.narration: Each anticodon is simply the complement of the codon, written in the opposite direction. Two different codons, U U U and U U C, are read by different transfer RNAs yet bring the same amino acid, phenylalanine. That is degeneracy, and it is why some base changes are silent.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Transcription unit: promoter, structural gene, terminator; template strand 3′→5′; RNA made 5′→3′.
Bacteria: one RNA polymerase (sigma, rho). Eukaryotes: polymerase I, II, III; hnRNA spliced, capped, tailed.
Exon, intron, cistron, recon, muton; monocistronic (eukaryotes) and polycistronic (bacteria).
Triplet code (64 codons; 61 sense, 3 stop): unambiguous, degenerate, comma-less, nearly universal; AUG starts.
Translation: charging, initiation at AUG, elongation (A and P sites, peptide bond by ribozyme), termination by release factor.

visual.alt: Summary table of where each step happens

slides.narration: To recap: a gene is transcribed from its template strand, the transcript is processed in eukaryotes, and the triplet code is read on ribosomes by transfer RNAs that bring the right amino acids until a stop codon is reached.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write strands with **5′ and 3′ ends**, and use **U, not T**, in RNA.
Define **intron, exon, cistron, recon and muton** in one line each.
Explain **degenerate** and **unambiguous** with an example.
Name the **A and P sites** and the role of the **release factor**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Always label the ends of strands and use uracil in RNA. Keep definitions of the gene terms short. Explain each feature of the code with an example. And describe translation in its three stages, naming the sites on the ribosome.

slides.heading: Regulation, genomes and fingerprints
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how genes are switched on and off, how the human genome was read, and how DNA identifies people.

visual.alt: Flow from gene regulation to the Human Genome Project to DNA fingerprinting

slides.narration: Cells do not express every gene all the time. We start with how bacteria switch genes on when needed, then see how the complete human sequence was read, and finally how differences in that sequence can identify a person.

slides.heading: Levels of gene regulation
slides.body_md: In eukaryotes expression can be regulated at several levels; in bacteria, control of **transcription initiation** is the main one.

rows: mRNA moving from nucleus to cytoplasm

visual.alt: Table of levels of regulation of gene expression

slides.narration: A bacterium growing on glucose does not need the enzymes that break down lactose. Switching their genes on only when lactose is present saves energy. Such switches act mainly on the start of transcription.

slides.heading: The lac operon
slides.body_md: Proposed by **Jacob and Monod**, the **lac operon** has a regulatory gene **i** (makes the **repressor**), the promoter **p**, the operator **o**, and structural genes **z** (β-galactosidase), **y** (permease) and **a** (transacetylase). **Lactose (allolactose)** is the **inducer**.

slides.heading: Human Genome Project: goals and methods
slides.body_md: Launched in **1990** and completed in **2003**, the Human Genome Project aimed to identify all genes, determine the sequence of the **3 billion base pairs**, store the data, and address **ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI)**.

rows: Identify all genes that are expressed as RNA
Sequence the whole genome, coding and non-coding, then assign functions
Cloning in BAC and YAC vectors
Align overlapping fragments into the full sequence

slides.narration: Two approaches were used. One identified the genes that are expressed as RNA, using expressed sequence tags. The other, sequence annotation, read the whole genome and then worked out what each part does. Fragments cloned in bacteria and yeast were read by machines and joined by computers.

slides.heading: Salient features of the human genome
slides.body_md: The human genome has about **3164.7 million** nucleotide bases.

visual.alt: Table of salient features of the human genome

slides.narration: Almost ninety nine percent of nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all people. Most of the genome does not code for proteins, and a large share consists of repeated sequences. The function of over half the discovered genes was not known when the project ended.

slides.body_md: If less than 2 percent of the 3164.7 million base pairs code for proteins, at most how many million base pairs are coding?

The remaining **more than 98 percent** includes introns, regulatory regions and repeats.

slides.narration: Two hundredths of about three thousand one hundred sixty five million is roughly sixty three million. So only a small fraction of our DNA directly codes for proteins; the rest has regulatory, structural or unknown roles.

slides.narration: The human sequence, together with those of model organisms, helps doctors find the genes behind disorders, guides new treatments, and lets biologists trace how genomes have changed over evolution.

slides.heading: DNA fingerprinting: the technique
slides.body_md: Developed by **Alec Jeffreys**, DNA fingerprinting compares **repetitive DNA**, especially **variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs)**, which differ in number between individuals. Repetitive DNA separates as **satellite DNA** in density-gradient centrifugation.

visual.alt: Flow of the steps of DNA fingerprinting

slides.narration: Because the number of repeats varies, the fragments cut out by restriction enzymes differ in size from person to person. After separation on a gel and transfer to a membrane, a labelled probe lights up the repeat-containing fragments as a pattern of bands unique to each individual, except identical twins.

sections.heading: 1. Transcription and processing
sections.body_md:
**Transcription** copies the information in one strand of DNA into RNA. A **transcription unit** has three regions: a **promoter** (upstream; RNA polymerase binds here), the **structural gene**, and a **terminator** (downstream). Of the two DNA strands, the one with polarity **3′→5′** acts as the **template strand**; the other (5′→3′) is the **coding strand**, whose sequence is the same as the RNA except that **thymine is replaced by uracil**. RNA is always made in the **5′→3′** direction. Both strands are not copied because the two RNAs would be complementary, pair up, and prevent translation.

**Stages:** initiation, elongation and termination. In **bacteria** a single DNA-dependent **RNA polymerase** makes all RNAs; the **sigma (σ) factor** helps initiation and the **rho (ρ) factor** helps termination. Transcription and translation can be coupled in the cytoplasm.

In **eukaryotes** there are three RNA polymerases in the nucleus: **RNA polymerase I** (rRNAs: 28S, 18S, 5.8S), **II** (**hnRNA**, the precursor of mRNA) and **III** (tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNAs).

**Processing of hnRNA** (in the nucleus):
- **Splicing:** introns (non-coding intervening sequences) are removed and exons (coding sequences) are joined.
- **Capping:** methyl guanosine triphosphate is added to the **5′ end**.
- **Tailing:** 200–300 adenylate residues (**poly-A tail**) are added to the **3′ end**.
The fully processed hnRNA, now **mRNA**, is transported to the cytoplasm. Genes with introns are **split genes**.

**Terms:** **exon** — coding sequence present in mature mRNA; **intron** — intervening sequence removed by splicing; **cistron** — segment of DNA coding for one polypeptide; **recon** — smallest unit capable of recombination; **muton** — smallest unit capable of mutation; **monocistronic** — one structural gene in a transcription unit (mostly eukaryotes); **polycistronic** — several structural genes in one unit (mostly bacteria).

Heterogeneous nuclear RNA: the primary transcript of eukaryotic structural genes before processing.
Removal of introns and joining of exons.
DNA segment coding for one polypeptide.

sections.heading: 2. The genetic code
sections.body_md:
The sequence of bases in mRNA determines the sequence of amino acids in a protein. **George Gamow** argued that with **4 bases** and **20 amino acids**, the code must be a **triplet**: 4³ = **64** combinations (a doublet gives only 4² = 16). **Har Gobind Khorana** developed chemical methods to synthesise RNA with defined base combinations; **Marshall Nirenberg** used a **cell-free system** for protein synthesis to decode codons; **Severo Ochoa**’s enzyme **polynucleotide phosphorylase** made RNA with defined sequences without a template.

**Features:**
1. The codon is a **triplet**; 61 codons code for amino acids and **3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons**.
2. One codon codes for only one amino acid: the code is **unambiguous and specific**.
3. Some amino acids have more than one codon: the code is **degenerate**.
4. The code is read in a continuous manner: it is **comma-less**.
5. The code is **nearly universal**: UUU codes for phenylalanine in bacteria and in humans (exceptions in mitochondria and some protozoans).
6. **AUG** has dual functions: it codes for **methionine** and acts as the **initiator codon**.

**Example (computed).** Template 3′–TACAAGCCTACCATT–5′ gives mRNA 5′–AUGUUCGGAUGGUAA–3′, which codes for **Met–Phe–Gly–Trp**, then stop.

key_terms.definition_md: Triplet of bases in mRNA coding for one amino acid or stop.
More than one codon for some amino acids.
AUG, which also codes for methionine.

rows: UUU and UUC both code for phenylalanine

sections.heading: 3. Translation
sections.body_md:
Translation is the polymerisation of amino acids into a polypeptide in the order set by mRNA codons, on **ribosomes** in the cytoplasm.

**tRNA — the adapter molecule.** tRNA has an **anticodon loop** with bases complementary to the codon and an **amino-acid acceptor end** (3′ end) to which the amino acid binds. Its secondary structure is a **clover leaf**; its 3-D structure is an **inverted L**. There are no tRNAs for stop codons.

**Steps:**
1. **Charging (aminoacylation):** each amino acid is activated in the presence of **ATP** and linked to its tRNA.
2. **Initiation:** the **small ribosomal subunit** binds mRNA; the initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with the **start codon AUG**; the large subunit joins.
3. **Elongation:** the ribosome has two sites for tRNAs. A charged tRNA whose anticodon matches the codon enters the **A site**; a **peptide bond** forms between the growing chain (on the tRNA in the **P site**) and the new amino acid; the **rRNA** of the large subunit (23S rRNA in bacteria) acts as the enzyme — a **ribozyme**. The ribosome then moves one codon towards the **3′ end** (translocation).
4. **Termination:** when a stop codon reaches the A site, a **release factor** binds and the polypeptide is released; the ribosome dissociates.

mRNA has **untranslated regions (UTRs)** before the start codon (5′ UTR) and after the stop codon (3′ UTR); they are needed for efficient translation.

key_terms.definition_md: Linking of an amino acid to its tRNA using ATP (charging).
Triplet on tRNA complementary to an mRNA codon.

sections.heading: 4. Regulation of gene expression: the lac operon
sections.body_md:
Gene expression in eukaryotes can be regulated at the levels of (i) transcription, (ii) processing (splicing), (iii) transport of mRNA from nucleus to cytoplasm and (iv) translation. In bacteria, control of **the rate of transcription initiation** is the main level.

An **operon** is a group of genes that are transcribed together and regulated as a unit. **François Jacob and Jacques Monod** first described the **lac operon** of *E. coli*:
- **i** — the **regulatory gene**, makes the **repressor** protein (constitutively; it has its own promoter);
- **p** — promoter; **o** — operator, where the repressor binds;
- **z** — **β-galactosidase**, which hydrolyses lactose into galactose and glucose; **y** — **permease**, which increases the permeability of the cell to lactose; **a** — **transacetylase**.

**No lactose:** the repressor binds the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes.
**Lactose present:** a few lactose molecules enter (low permease level); lactose (strictly **allolactose**) acts as the **inducer**, binds the repressor and **inactivates** it, so it cannot bind the operator; RNA polymerase transcribes z, y and a as one **polycistronic** mRNA. When lactose is used up, the repressor binds again. This is **negative regulation**, since the repressor switches the operon off.

key_terms.definition_md: Group of genes transcribed together and regulated as a unit.
Substance (lactose, allolactose) that inactivates the repressor and switches on the lac operon.
Protein made by gene i that binds the operator and blocks transcription.

sections.heading: 5. The Human Genome Project
sections.body_md:
The **Human Genome Project (HGP)**, launched in **1990** and completed in **2003**, was coordinated by the US Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health, with the UK, Japan, France, Germany, China and others.

**Goals:** identify all the genes (about 20 000–25 000) in human DNA; determine the sequence of the **3 billion** chemical base pairs; store the information in databases; improve tools for data analysis; transfer related technologies to other sectors; and address the **ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI)** that may arise.

**Methodologies:** (i) **Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs)** — identifying all the genes that are expressed as RNA; (ii) **sequence annotation** — sequencing the whole set of the genome, coding and non-coding, and later assigning functions to different regions. Total DNA was broken into fragments, cloned in hosts using **BAC** (bacterial artificial chromosome) and **YAC** (yeast artificial chromosome) vectors, sequenced with **automated DNA sequencers** (Frederick Sanger’s method) and arranged by specialised computer programs using overlapping regions.

**Salient features:**
- The genome has **3164.7 million** nucleotide bases.
- The total number of genes was estimated at about **30 000** (later estimates nearer 20 000).
- The average gene has **3000 bases**; the largest known gene, **dystrophin**, has **2.4 million** bases.
- Almost **99.9 percent** of bases are the same in all people.
- The functions of over half the discovered genes were unknown.
- **Less than 2 percent** of the genome codes for proteins — at most about **63.3 million** bp.
- **Repeated sequences** make up a very large portion of the genome.
- **Chromosome 1** has the most genes (**2968**) and **Y** the fewest (**231**).
- About **1.4 million** locations of single-base DNA differences, **single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)**, were identified.

**Applications:** finding the genes behind disorders, designing new diagnosis and treatment (including gene therapy), understanding human biology and evolution; the sequences of other organisms (bacteria, yeast, *Caenorhabditis elegans*, *Drosophila*, rice, *Arabidopsis*) were also completed.

key_terms.definition_md: Expressed sequence tag: a short sequence used to identify a gene expressed as RNA.
Sequencing the whole genome and then assigning functions to its regions.
Single nucleotide polymorphism: a single-base difference between individuals.
Bacterial and yeast artificial chromosomes used as cloning vectors.

sections.heading: 6. DNA fingerprinting
sections.body_md:
About 99.9 percent of the human sequence is the same in everyone; DNA fingerprinting compares the differences in **repetitive DNA**. Repetitive DNA separates from the bulk DNA as **satellite DNA** peaks in density-gradient centrifugation. Satellite DNA is classified as **micro-satellites** and **mini-satellites** by length and base composition; it does not code for proteins and shows **high polymorphism**.

**Variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs)** — mini-satellites in which a short sequence is repeated many times — differ in **copy number** from person to person, so the size of the DNA fragment containing them differs. The technique was developed by **Alec Jeffreys**, who used a VNTR as a probe.

**Steps:** (i) **isolation** of DNA; (ii) **digestion** with restriction endonucleases; (iii) separation of fragments by **gel electrophoresis**; (iv) **Southern blotting** — transfer to a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane; (v) **hybridisation** with a labelled **VNTR probe**; (vi) detection by **autoradiography**. The pattern of bands is the **DNA fingerprint**; it is unique to each individual except identical twins. Small samples can be amplified by **PCR** first.

**Applications:** forensic science (identifying suspects from blood, hair, semen or skin), **paternity and maternity** disputes, identification of disaster victims, studies of population and genetic diversity and evolution.

**Ethical issues:** genetic data reveal private information about a person and relatives; samples need **informed consent**; databases need **secure storage and controlled access**; misuse could lead to **discrimination** (for example by employers or insurers); results must be handled carefully in court.

key_terms.definition_md: Variable number tandem repeat: a mini-satellite whose repeat number varies between individuals.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing T instead of U in mRNA, or forgetting the 5′ and 3′ ends.
- Saying the coding strand is copied (the template strand is copied; the RNA has the coding-strand sequence).
- Calling the code ambiguous because it is degenerate (one codon → one amino acid; one amino acid → several codons).
- Saying lactose binds the operator (it binds the repressor).
- Mixing up ESTs (expressed genes) with sequence annotation (whole genome).
- Leaving out Southern blotting or hybridisation from the fingerprinting steps.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term (cistron, muton), a codon, an enzyme of the lac operon, a step of fingerprinting.
- 2–3-mark questions: processing of hnRNA; features of the code; lac operon on and off; ESTs vs annotation; paternity gel.
- 5-mark questions in parts: transcription unit with diagram; translation steps; lac operon with labelled diagram; DNA fingerprinting with uses and ethics.

answer.model_answer_md: Template strand: **3′–TACGGCAAT–5′**; mRNA: **5′–AUGCCGUUA–3′**. The **template strand** is the one actually **copied** by RNA polymerase; the **coding strand** is **not copied**, but its sequence is the same as the mRNA (with T in place of U), so it is used to write the code.

questions.solution_md: Strands and roles.

questions.stem_md: A researcher compares the hnRNA and the mature mRNA of the same human gene. The mRNA is shorter in the middle, but has an extra group at one end and a long run of adenine nucleotides at the other. Explain these three differences.

answer.model_answer_md: **Splicing** removed the **introns** from the middle of the hnRNA and joined the **exons**, so the mRNA is shorter. **Capping** added **methyl guanosine triphosphate** to the **5′ end**. **Tailing** added a **poly-A tail** of **200–300 adenylate** residues to the **3′ end**. All three steps take place in the **nucleus** before the mRNA moves to the cytoplasm.

questions.solution_md: Splicing, capping, tailing.

questions.stem_md: Describe the three stages of transcription in bacteria, stating the roles of the sigma and rho factors.

answer.model_answer_md: **Initiation:** RNA polymerase, helped by the **sigma (σ) factor**, binds the **promoter** and starts copying the template strand. **Elongation:** the polymerase moves along the template, adding **ribonucleoside triphosphates** complementary to it and making RNA **5′→3′**; the enzyme also unwinds the helix ahead. **Termination:** at the **terminator**, the **rho (ρ) factor** helps the polymerase stop and release the RNA. A single RNA polymerase makes **all types of RNA** in bacteria.

questions.solution_md: Three stages.

questions.stem_md: A toxin from a mushroom blocks RNA polymerase II in human liver cells. Which kinds of RNA will still be made, which will not, and why will the cell soon stop making new proteins coded by nuclear genes?

answer.model_answer_md: **RNA polymerase I** (large rRNAs) and **III** (tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNAs) still work, so these RNAs are **still made**. **RNA polymerase II** makes **hnRNA**, the precursor of **mRNA**, so **no new mRNA** is made. Without new mRNA, ribosomes have **no fresh message** to translate, so new proteins stop appearing once old mRNA is used up.

questions.solution_md: Polymerase II makes hnRNA.

marking_scheme.step: Polymerase I and III products still made
No mRNA, so no new protein

questions.stem_md: An hnRNA of 3200 nucleotides contains three introns of 450, 600 and 350 nucleotides. Ignoring the cap and tail, how many nucleotides remain in the spliced mRNA?

(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a transcription unit showing the promoter, structural gene, terminator, and the template and coding strands with their polarity. [2]
(b) Why is only one strand of DNA transcribed? [1]
(c) A template strand reads 3′–TACGGATTC–5′. Write the mRNA, and state the changes it would undergo in a eukaryotic nucleus before translation. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a DNA double helix with the **promoter** upstream, the **structural gene** in the middle and the **terminator** downstream; the **template strand** marked **3′→5′** and the **coding strand** 5′→3′; RNA shown being made **5′→3′**.

(b) If both strands were copied, the two RNAs would be **complementary**, would **pair** to form double-stranded RNA and would **not be translated**.

(c) mRNA: **5′–AUGCCUAAG–3′**. In the nucleus the transcript (hnRNA) would undergo **splicing** (introns removed), **capping** (methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5′ end) and **tailing** (poly-A at the 3′ end).

questions.solution_md: Diagram; reason; mRNA and processing.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The genetic code is degenerate.

**Reason (R):** One codon codes for more than one amino acid.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: some amino acids have several codons. R is false: each codon codes for only one amino acid (the code is unambiguous) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A human gene for a hormone is placed in E. coli, and the bacterium makes the correct human polypeptide. Which feature of the genetic code makes this possible?
questions.solution_md: The same codons code for the same amino acids in bacteria and humans — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Gamow argued that a code of two bases per codon could not specify all the amino acids in proteins. Why?

options.text_md: It would give 64 codons, too many for 20 amino acids.
Two bases cannot pair with each other.
RNA has only two kinds of bases.
It would give only 16 codons for 20 amino acids.

questions.solution_md: With 4 bases, a doublet gives $4^{2} = 16$ words, fewer than 20; a triplet gives $4^{3} = 64$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which enzyme, studied by Severo Ochoa, was used to make RNA molecules of defined sequence without a template?
questions.solution_md: Ochoa’s polynucleotide phosphorylase polymerised RNA in a template-independent manner — option (d).

questions.stem_md: One extra base is inserted just after the start codon of a gene, and every amino acid after that point changes. Which feature of the genetic code explains this?

options.text_md: It is comma-less, read continuously in triplets from a fixed start.
It has a dual-function start codon.

questions.solution_md: With no gaps between codons, an insertion shifts the reading frame of every later triplet — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Imagine an organism whose genetic code used codons of four bases each, still with four kinds of base. How many different codons could it have?
The three stop codons of the genetic code are UAA, UAG and ______.
questions.solution_md: UGA.

questions.stem_md: How many amino acids are in the peptide coded by the mRNA 5′–AUGGCUUCAGGAUAGCC–3′, reading from the first AUG?
questions.solution_md: Codons AUG GCU UCA GGA then UAG (stop): Met, Ala, Ser, Gly; number $= 4$.

questions.stem_md: State four salient features of the genetic code.

answer.model_answer_md: The code is **triplet** (three bases per codon); **unambiguous and specific** (one codon, one amino acid); **degenerate** (some amino acids have more than one codon); **comma-less**; **nearly universal**; and **AUG** both codes for methionine and **starts** translation, while **UAA, UAG, UGA** stop it.

questions.solution_md: Four features.

questions.stem_md: An mRNA has one AUG codon near its 5′ end and another in the middle of its coding region. Explain why the first acts as a start codon while the second simply codes for methionine within the chain.

answer.model_answer_md: AUG has a **dual function**. The **first AUG** after the 5′ untranslated region is where the **small ribosomal subunit** and the **initiator tRNA** assemble, so it **sets the reading frame** and starts translation. Later AUGs are read **in frame** during elongation and simply add **methionine** to the chain.

questions.solution_md: Dual function of AUG.

marking_scheme.step: First AUG: initiation and reading frame

questions.stem_md: Explain the contributions of George Gamow, Har Gobind Khorana and Marshall Nirenberg to deciphering the genetic code.

answer.model_answer_md: **Gamow** argued that with **four bases** coding for **20 amino acids**, a codon must have **three bases** (4³ = 64 combinations; a doublet gives only 16). **Khorana** developed **chemical methods** to synthesise RNA molecules with **defined combinations of bases** (repeats), whose products revealed codons. **Nirenberg** used a **cell-free system** for protein synthesis to find which amino acid each codon specified, which finally helped decode the code.

questions.solution_md: Three contributions.

questions.stem_md: The codon UUU in a gene changes to UUC in one person and to UAU in another. Using the genetic code, predict the effect of each change on the protein and name the feature of the code shown by the first change.

answer.model_answer_md: UUU codes for **Phe**. **UUC** also codes for **Phe**, so the protein is **unchanged** (a silent change) — this shows the code is **degenerate**. **UAU** codes for **Tyr**, so one amino acid is **replaced** by another, which may change the protein’s shape and function.

questions.solution_md: Silent vs substitution.

marking_scheme.step: UAU gives Tyr: amino acid replaced

questions.stem_md: What happens during aminoacylation of tRNA?

options.text_md: Each tRNA is linked to its specific amino acid, using energy from ATP.
The tRNA anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon.
Two amino acids are joined by a peptide bond.
Introns are removed from the tRNA precursor.

questions.solution_md: Aminoacylation, or charging, activates amino acids and attaches them to their tRNAs — option (a).

questions.stem_md: During elongation, a newly arriving charged tRNA carrying the next amino acid first binds the ribosome at the
questions.solution_md: The incoming aminoacyl-tRNA enters the A site; the growing chain is held in the P site — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In bacterial ribosomes, which molecule catalyses the formation of peptide bonds?
questions.solution_md: The 23S rRNA of the large subunit is the catalyst — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A ribosome translating an mRNA reaches the codon UAG in its A site. What happens next?

options.text_md: A tRNA carrying tyrosine binds the codon.
A release factor binds, and the polypeptide is released from the ribosome.
The ribosome moves back to the start codon.

questions.solution_md: UAG is a stop codon; no tRNA reads it, so a release factor ends translation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A codon on an mRNA reads 5′–GCA–3′. Which anticodon, written 3′→5′, does the matching tRNA carry?
questions.solution_md: The anticodon pairs base by base: G–C, C–G, A–U, giving CGU — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An mRNA has untranslated regions before the start codon and after the stop codon.

**Reason (R):** There is no tRNA that reads a stop codon.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the absence of tRNAs for stop codons does not explain why mRNAs have untranslated regions, which are needed for efficient translation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The secondary structure of tRNA is drawn as a ______ leaf, while its three-dimensional shape is an inverted L.
questions.solution_md: Clover (clover-leaf structure).

questions.stem_md: A tRNA molecule has the anticodon 3′–UAC–5′. Which mRNA codon does it read, and which amino acid does it carry? Why is tRNA called an adapter molecule?

answer.model_answer_md: It reads the codon **5′–AUG–3′**, which codes for **Met** (methionine; it is the start codon). tRNA is an **adapter** because it **reads the codon** with its anticodon and also **carries the matching amino acid**, linking the language of bases to that of amino acids.

questions.solution_md: AUG, methionine; adapter.

questions.stem_md: Describe the initiation, elongation and termination stages of translation in bacteria.

answer.model_answer_md: **Initiation:** the **small ribosomal subunit** binds the mRNA; the **initiator tRNA** carrying **methionine** pairs with the **start codon AUG**, and the large subunit joins. **Elongation:** a charged tRNA whose anticodon matches the next codon enters the **A site**; a **peptide bond** forms with the chain held in the **P site**, catalysed by **rRNA (ribozyme)**; the ribosome then **moves one codon** towards the 3′ end. **Termination:** at a **stop codon** a **release factor** binds, the polypeptide is released and the ribosome separates.

questions.solution_md: Three stages.

marking_scheme.step: Elongation: A and P sites, peptide bond, translocation

questions.stem_md:
(a) The template strand of a short gene reads 3′–TACAAGCCTACCATT–5′. Write the mRNA and the sequence of amino acids it codes for. [2]
(b) Explain the roles of the A site and the P site of the ribosome, and name the molecule that forms peptide bonds. [2]
(c) Why is there no tRNA for the last codon of this mRNA? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) mRNA **5′–AUGUUCGGAUGGUAA–3′**; codons AUG UUC GGA UGG UAA; peptide **Met–Phe–Gly–Trp**, then **stop**.

(b) The **A site** receives each new **charged tRNA** whose anticodon matches the codon; the **P site** holds the tRNA carrying the **growing chain**. The chain is transferred to the new amino acid by a **peptide bond**, formed by the **rRNA of the large subunit** acting as a **ribozyme**; the ribosome then moves one codon on.

(c) The last codon, **UAA**, is a **stop codon**; it codes for no amino acid, so it is recognised by a **release factor**, not a tRNA.

questions.solution_md: mRNA and peptide; ribosome sites; stop codon.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Stop codon read by release factor

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Regulation of the lac operon by its repressor is described as negative regulation.

**Reason (R):** The repressor protein is coded by the regulatory gene i.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the source of the repressor does not explain why the control is negative; it is negative because the repressor switches the operon off — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the absence of lactose, RNA polymerase cannot transcribe the lac structural genes.

**Reason (R):** Lactose binds directly to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the repressor binds the operator; lactose binds the repressor and removes it — option (c).

questions.stem_md: What is an operon? Name the three structural genes of the lac operon and the enzyme coded by each.

answer.model_answer_md: An **operon** is a group of genes **transcribed together** and **regulated as a unit**. Lac structural genes: **z** — **β-galactosidase**; **y** — **permease**; **a** — **transacetylase**.

questions.solution_md: Definition and three genes.

questions.stem_md: Lactose is added to a culture of E. coli that had been growing without it, and some hours later all the lactose has been used up. Explain the changes in the lac operon during this time.

answer.model_answer_md: Before lactose, the **repressor** (from gene **i**) is bound to the **operator**, so the operon is **off**. When lactose enters, a few molecules taken up by a low level of permease act as the **inducer** (allolactose): it **binds the repressor**, which changes shape and **leaves the operator**. RNA polymerase now transcribes **z, y and a**, and the enzymes break down lactose. When **lactose is used up**, the free repressor **binds the operator again** and the operon is **switched off**.

questions.solution_md: Off, on, off.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of the lac operon in the absence of lactose. [2]
(b) Explain how the operon is switched on when lactose is present. [2]
(c) Predict what would happen in a mutant whose operator cannot bind the repressor. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** gene **i** making the **repressor**; **promoter (p)**, **operator (o)** with the repressor **bound**; structural genes **z, y, a**; RNA polymerase **blocked**; no mRNA.

(b) **Lactose (allolactose)** enters and acts as the **inducer**: it **binds the repressor** and **inactivates** it, so the repressor **cannot bind the operator**. **RNA polymerase** binds the promoter and transcribes **z, y and a** as one **polycistronic mRNA**, giving β-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase.

(c) The repressor could never block transcription, so the structural genes would be **transcribed all the time**, even **without lactose**.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; switching on; operator mutant.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
Four strains of E. coli were grown with and without lactose, and β-galactosidase activity was measured.

| Strain | Change | No lactose | Lactose present |
|---|---|---|---|
| W | None (wild type) | Absent | High |
| X | Gene i cannot make repressor | High | High |
| Y | Operator cannot bind repressor | High | High |
| Z | Gene z mutated | Absent | Absent |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) The repressor is bound to the operator.

**(b)** (c) In both, the repressor never stays on the operator, so transcription is always on.

**(c)** (i) The operon **is transcribed** when lactose inactivates the repressor, but gene **z** is **mutated**, so the mRNA codes for a **non-functional** (or no) **β-galactosidase**. Regulation is normal; the **structural gene product** is faulty.

**OR** (ii) Strain W makes the lactose enzymes **only when lactose is present**, so it **saves energy and materials**. Strains X and Y make the enzymes **all the time**, **wasting resources** when there is no lactose to use.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** In the wild type, the free repressor blocks transcription — option (b).

**(b)** No repressor (X) or an operator that cannot hold it (Y) both leave the operon permanently on — option (c).

**(c)** (i) Faulty structural gene.

(ii) Saving energy.

questions.stem_md: State four goals of the Human Genome Project.

answer.model_answer_md: To **identify all the genes** in human DNA; to **determine the sequence** of the **3 billion** base pairs; to **store the information** in databases; to **improve tools for data analysis**; to **transfer technologies** to other sectors; and to address the **ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI)**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the two approaches used in the Human Genome Project, and outline how DNA fragments were sequenced and assembled.

answer.model_answer_md: **Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs)** identify **all the genes expressed as RNA**. **Sequence annotation** sequences the **whole genome**, coding and non-coding, and later **assigns functions** to regions. For sequencing, total DNA was **broken into fragments**, **cloned** in **BAC and YAC** vectors, read by **automated sequencers** (Sanger’s method), and arranged into the full sequence by **computer programs** using **overlapping regions**.

questions.stem_md: State six salient features of the human genome revealed by the Human Genome Project.

answer.model_answer_md: It has **3164.7 million** bases; about **30 000 genes** were estimated; the **average gene** has **3000 bases** and the largest, **dystrophin**, **2.4 million**; **99.9 percent** of bases are the same in all people; **less than 2 percent** codes for proteins; **repeated sequences** form a large part; **chromosome 1** has the most genes (2968) and **Y** the fewest (231); about **1.4 million SNPs** were found.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Identify all genes**; **sequence the 3 billion base pairs**; **store data** in databases; **improve analysis tools**; **transfer technology**; address **ethical, legal and social issues**.

(b) **Expressed sequence tags** identify all genes expressed as RNA. **Sequence annotation** sequences the whole genome, coding and non-coding, and then assigns functions; DNA fragments were cloned in **BAC/YAC** vectors, sequenced automatically and assembled by computer from overlapping sequences.

(c) **Genetic testing** could tell family members whether they **carry the allele**, guide **genetic counselling** before having children, and point to **early diagnosis** or targeted treatment such as **gene therapy**.

questions.stem_md: A city plans to keep the DNA fingerprints of everyone who is arrested, even if they are not charged. State two ethical issues this raises and a safeguard for each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Privacy:** genetic data reveal information about a person and their **relatives**; safeguard — **secure storage** with **controlled access**. **Consent and misuse:** people not charged have not agreed, and data could be used for **discrimination**; safeguard — **informed consent** or **deletion** of records when no charge is made, backed by **law**.

questions.solution_md: Two issues and safeguards.

questions.stem_md: List, in order, the steps of DNA fingerprinting, and state the purpose of the labelled probe.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Isolation** of DNA; (ii) **digestion** with **restriction endonucleases**; (iii) separation of fragments by **gel electrophoresis**; (iv) **Southern blotting** onto a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane; (v) **hybridisation** with a **labelled VNTR probe**; (vi) **autoradiography** to see the bands. The **probe** binds only to fragments carrying the **complementary repeat**, so only those fragments show up as bands.

questions.solution_md: Six steps; probe.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs), and why are they useful in identifying people? [2]
(b) Describe the steps used to obtain a DNA fingerprint. [2]
(c) A blood stain is found at a crime scene and three suspects are held. Explain how the fingerprints would be used. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **VNTRs** are **mini-satellites** in which a short DNA sequence is **repeated in tandem**; the **number of repeats** varies between individuals, so the **fragments** containing them differ in **size**, giving a pattern **unique** to each person (except identical twins).

(b) DNA is **isolated**, cut with **restriction enzymes**, separated by **gel electrophoresis**, transferred by **Southern blotting**, **hybridised** with a **labelled VNTR probe** and detected by **autoradiography**.

(c) The fingerprint from the **stain** is compared with those of the **three suspects**; a suspect whose **band pattern matches exactly** is linked to the scene, while non-matching suspects are **excluded**.

questions.passage_md: In a paternity dispute, DNA fingerprints were prepared from a mother, her child and two men, P and Q, using the same VNTR probe. The gel is shown in the figure.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 2

**(b)** (a) Man P

**(c)** (i) A child inherits **half** of its VNTR alleles from **each parent**. Removing the bands it shares with the **mother** leaves the **paternal** bands, which **must all** be present in the **biological father**.

**OR** (ii) Unrelated people can **share some bands** by chance, because many people carry the same repeat number at a locus. Paternity needs **all** the non-maternal bands to match, usually across **several probes**.

**(b)** All 2 non-maternal bands of the child are in man P, and 0 are in man Q — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Half from each parent.

(ii) Chance sharing.
